title: Cognitive Integrity Framework: Computational Validation and Empirical Analysis (Part 2 of 3: Implementation, Empirical Analysis, and Adversarial Evaluation)
description: This paper presents the computational validation of the Cognitive Integrity Framework (CIF) whose formal foundations are established in Part 1 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18364119). We implement the CIF defense suite --- cognitive firewalls, belief sandboxes, tripwires, drift and anomaly scoring, trust calculus with bounded delegation, provenance tracking, and Byzantine-tolerant consensus --- and evaluate it on an integrated 1,475-item attack corpus spanning fifteen categories, together with a 120-item benign corpus whose harder half carries attack-adjacent vocabulary. Multi-tier evaluation. Real pipeline evaluation across 30 seeds yields a mean detection rate of 86.3% (95% CI 85.5%-87.1%) at an 18.5% false-positive rate on the Claude Code architecture, measured on an injection-only 100-sample-per-seed arm. LLM-backed validation (N=10, Gemma 3 4B) reaches 80-100% across two topologies and is reported as preliminary and underpowered. Colony benchmarks at 20-100 agents reach 81-100% on structured adversarial scenarios, with emergent misalignment the hardest case at 74.3% detection and a 25.5% false-positive rate. Parametric simulation (N=3,800) characterises a 96-100% design-level ceiling across four production architectures, and is labelled a simulation rather than a measurement wherever it appears. Ablation on a 100-attack corpus attributes almost all marginal detection to the Invariants module: the full pipeline reaches 89.0% true-positive rate, removing Invariants costs 65 percentage points, removing the Tripwire costs two, and removing any other module costs nothing the corpus can measure. The layered architecture is therefore only partly borne out, and the paper says so. An undefended control arm places the defense's cost at +0.610 ms at the median and +32 KiB peak. Measured as ranked scorers, the drift score and the firewall pattern matcher fall below chance (AUC 0.374 and 0.383, intervals excluding 0.5). Every quantity the three papers share is derived from a single ledger and gated in continuous integration; no reported number is typed by hand. All experiments are deterministically reproducible at seed 42, and the code, corpora and artifacts are at https://github.com/docxology/cognitive_integrity. This is Part 2 of the three-part Cognitive Security for Multiagent Operators series: - Part 1 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18364119): formal foundations and theoretical analysis - Part 2 (this paper): computational validation and implementation - Part 3+4 merged (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18364130): unified practitioner guidance and cross-domain applications

methods.name: Python implementation of the CIF defense suite
methods.description: Cognitive firewalls, belief sandboxes, trust calculus with bounded delegation, tripwires, behavioral invariants and Byzantine-tolerant consensus were built as tested modules.
methods.evidence: We implemented the CIF defense suite—cognitive firewalls, belief sandboxes, trust calculus with bounded delegation, tripwire detection, behavioral invariants, and Byzantine-tolerant consensus—as tested Python modules

methods.name: Synthetic template-generated attack corpus (seed 42)
methods.description: Attacks are generated by deterministic template expansion, not drawn from published benchmarks; the paper describes both a 950-item and a 1,475-item integrated version.
methods.evidence: Corpus provenance: The 950 attacks are entirely synthetic — generated by deterministic template expansion. No attacks in this corpus are drawn from JailbreakBench, PromptInject, TensorTrust, or any other published benchmark dataset.

methods.name: Multi-seed pipeline evaluation and leave-one-out ablation studies
methods.description: The real pipeline was run across 30 seeds on an injection-only arm, and ablations on a 100-attack corpus measured each module's marginal contribution.
methods.evidence: real defense pipeline evaluation across 30 random seeds, yielding a mean detection rate of 86.3% [95% CI: 85.5%, 87.1%] at a 18.5% false-positive rate on the Claude Code architecture

methods.name: LLM-backed multiagent validation with Gemma 3 4B via Ollama (N=10)
methods.description: A small LLM-backed arm tested Claude Code and CrewAI topologies; the author reports it as preliminary and underpowered.
methods.evidence: LLM-backed multiagent validation (𝑁= 10, Gemma 3 4B via Ollama) achieving 80–100% detection across Claude Code and CrewAI topologies; this arm is preliminary and underpowered

methods.name: Colony benchmarks (20-100 agents) and parametric simulation (N=3,800)
methods.description: Structured adversarial colony scenarios and a calibrated parametric simulation across four architectures characterize scale behavior and the design-level ceiling.
methods.evidence: (4) colony benchmarks at scale (20–100 agents) demonstrating 81–100% detection on structured adversarial scenarios; and (5) large- scale parametric simulation (𝑁= 3,800)

key_findings: Ablation identified the Invariants module as the highest-marginal-contribution component (delta TPR = -0.650 when removed, 73% of pipeline detection).
The author reports a 9.7-11 percentage-point gap between the parametric ceiling (96-100%) and measured pipeline performance (86.3% multi-seed, 89.0% ablation).
The layered defense architecture is only partly borne out: the strongest pairwise synergies were about +0.050, far below the Invariants module's contribution.
Trust decay with bounded delegation prevented trust amplification, with 100% sybil detection at 0% FPR in colony-scale simulation.
Emergent misalignment without explicit adversaries was the hardest colony scenario (74.3% detection, 25.5% FPR).
key_findings_evidence: identifying the Invariants module as the highest-marginal-contribution component (ΔTPR = −0.650 when removed, accounting for 73% of pipeline detection)
The gap between the parametric ceiling (96–100%) and current pipeline performance (86.3% multi-seed, 89.0% on the ablation corpus) is 9.7 to 11 percentage points
The layered defense architecture is only partly borne out: ablation studies show that a single component, the Invariants module, accounts for the majority of marginal detection on the ablation corpus

Trust decay with bounded delegation (𝛿𝑑) prevents trust amplification across all architectures—a structural guarantee verified both formally (Part 1) and through colony-scale simulation (100% sybil detection at 0% FPR).
Colony benchmarks reveal that emergent misalignment (agents collectively drifting without explicit adversaries) remains the most challenging scenario (74.3% detection, 25.5% FPR)

summary_provenance.notes: Part 2 of a 3-part series; attack corpus is fully synthetic. INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY in full text: corpus is described as 950 attacks / 4 categories (Sec. 9, Conclusion) and as 1,475 attacks / 5 categories / 15 subcategories (contributions list, Sec. 9.1, Sec. on generation); Table 19 says 950 is the extended=False corpus and 1,475 is the current default. README abstract uses 1,475/fifteen categories plus a 120-item benign corpus and cites Part 1 DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18364119 and Part 3+4 DOI 18364130, whereas the PDF abstract cites 22134544 and 22134548. Abstract gives the parametric-empirical gap as '9.7 to 11' pp vs '10–11' pp in the Conclusion. LLM arm underpowered (required N>=245); reformulation resistance not directly measured.
